question: What regulatory or legal problems do robotic construction processes run into?

answer.answer:
Compliance is a precondition rather than an afterthought: regulatory/legal concern (RI18) sits upstream of bespoke DFAB technology (AT3), additive manufacturing (PR3), on-site DFAB (PR8) and human-robot interaction (CO6), so each of those has to clear a standards or approval hurdle before it runs. The named problems are three: baseline robot safety compliance for anything a person works alongside, structural, fire and durability certification for 3D printed walls, and an alternative-means approval route for on-site printing where no prescriptive code exists. Work safety concern (RI20) is the exposure behind the safety rules, and the three cited ways of reducing it are human-robot interaction (CO6) under power-and-force limits, 3D scanning/RFID/sensing (CO2) for separation monitoring, and human assistance (AT10) as a wearable device. Watch the unevenness: of the four routes into regulatory/legal concern visible here, only the one from bespoke DFAB technology is carried by more than a couple of cases, and robotic drilling (PR19) and unmanned mobile vehicle (RE15) carry no cited edge at all, so the literature has simply not connected them to regulation yet.

**Where the regulatory burden lands**

12 of the 50 coded cases draw on RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern" (Risk), and it carries 5 cited dependency edges in total [1]; four of those five appear in the material in front of me, all of them standard-graded and all of them running into RI18, meaning compliance is the requirement and the technology or process is what waits on it.

- AT3 "Bespoke DFAB technology" (Attribute) dependsOn RI18, carried by 9 of the 50 coded cases: robot technology design and integration depends on baseline safety-standard compliance. [1] This is the most widely carried of the four.
- CO6 "Human-robot interaction" (Condition) dependsOn RI18, carried by 2 of the 50: human-robot collaborative work depends on compliance with robot safety standards. [1] The gap is worth noting: 32 of the 50 cases draw on CO6 [1], but only 2 carry this compliance edge with it.
- PR3 "Additive manufacturing" (Process) dependsOn RI18, carried by 2 of the 50: 3D printed concrete walls require certification against acceptance criteria for structural strength, fire safety and durability. [1]
- PR8 "On-site DFAB" (Process) dependsOn RI18, carried by 2 of the 50: on-site 3D concrete printing deployment proceeds via an alternative-means approval pathway. [1]

All four are backed by standards rather than by peer-reviewed study, which is consistent with their being compliance facts rather than empirical findings. Note also that these counts share a target (RI18) and so are comparable against that anchor; they say nothing about the enablers' importance in general.

**The safety exposure the rules exist to control**

RI20 "Work safety concern" (Risk) carries 3 inbound and 0 outbound dependency edges, all of them listed, and 13 of the 50 coded cases draw on it. [1] All three inbound edges are mitigations, so of RI20's own cited routes: AT10 "Human assistance" mitigates it, carried by 8 of the 50, via a passive exoskeleton that reduced lumbar erector spinae activity by 11 to 33 per cent MVC [1]; CO2 "3D scanning/RFID/sensing" mitigates it, carried by 7 of the 50, through speed-and-separation monitoring that maintains a minimum protective distance [1]; and CO6 "Human-robot interaction" mitigates it, carried by 4 of the 50, through power-and-force-limiting operation within biomechanical limits [1]. Two of the three are technical controls tied directly to the collaborative-robot standard; the third is protective equipment on the worker.

A second, non-safety condition attaches to human-robot work: CO6 also dependsOn RI6 "Require workforce training", carried by 27 of the 50, because the success of human-robot collaboration is contingent on a skilled workforce [1]. That is the most carried requirement on CO6 by a wide margin, which suggests the practical obstacle in the record is competence as much as certification.

**What the deployed record shows**

The census records retrieved here are dominated by regulation as an adoption driver, though the context links them to adoption reasons and not to individual enablers, so I cannot say which enablers any of them draws on.

- census_RXH5-1 was adopted to address regulation, performs assembly, steelwork and welding on the structural core, and is at technology readiness level 9 [2]; it is manufactured by Firm_027 and uses steel [3]. This is the mature, high-readiness end: regulation is a driver of adoption, not a blocker.
- On the additive-manufacturing route, census_RXM4-3 was adopted to address regulation, performs 3D printing, assembly and concrete work on the structural core, at technology readiness level 7 [4], and it is manufactured by Firm_115, uses concrete, and is the census record of RP15 [3]. RP15 itself is deployed as a mobile robot and off-site, at technology readiness level 7 [5]. The lower readiness here, against level 9 for the steel assembly records, sits alongside the certification demand that the printed-wall edge describes, though the context does not assert a causal link.
- census_RXT4-1 was adopted to address integration, market and regulation, performs assembly, material handling and timber joinery cutting on the structural core, at technology readiness level 9 [6]; it was developed by Firm_174 and uses timber [3].
- RP5 was adopted to address cost, integration and regulation, works on the structural core, is deployed off-site, and is at technology readiness level 9 [7], with census record census_RXH9-1b, manufactured by Firm_160, using timber [3].

**Limits on what can be claimed**

The widening of "robotic construction processes" to several enablers matters here, because two of them are outside the cited dependency layer entirely: 9 of the 50 coded cases draw on PR19 "Robotic drilling", and it carries no dependency edges [1], and 25 of the 50 draw on RE15 "Unmanned mobile vehicle", also with no dependency edges [1]. The cited layer is sparse and uneven, with 100 edges touching 68 of the 140 enablers, which is a property of the literature and not of the record [1], and 60% of Risks carry no edge at all [1]. So the absence of a regulatory edge on drilling or on mobile vehicles is an absence of published connection, not evidence that those processes face no legal friction. A related constraint sits in the same edgeless state: 25 of the 50 cases draw on RI19 "Production/assembly restriction", and it carries no dependency edges [1].

Finally, one of RI18's five cited edges is not in front of me, so this account of its connections is not complete, and the retrieved material does not establish which statutes or certification schemes beyond those named apply.

**Deployed evidence.** Selected by filtering the coded records, not by similarity. 15 records in the graph carry Regulation as their adoption driver; all are listed below.
- RP10, adopted to address integration, regulation; performs assembly, steelwork, welding; works on the structural core; deployed off-site; at technology readiness level 9.
- RP15, adopted to address regulation; performs 3d printing, assembly, concrete work; works on the structural core; deployed as a mobile robot, off-site; at technology readiness level 7.
- RP5, adopted to address cost, integration, regulation; works on the structural core; deployed off-site; at technology readiness level 9.
- census_RXH12-1, adopted to address quality, integration, regulation; performs assembly, timber joinery cutting; works on the structural core; at technology readiness level 9.
- census_RXH13-1, adopted to address regulation; performs assembly, steelwork, welding; works on the structural core; at technology readiness level 9.
- census_RXH5-1, adopted to address regulation; performs assembly, steelwork, welding; works on the structural core; at technology readiness level 9.
- census_RXH9-1b, adopted to address cost, integration, regulation; works on the structural core; at technology readiness level 9.
- census_RXM1-1, adopted to address regulation; performs inspection; at technology readiness level 7.
- census_RXM29-4, adopted to address integration, regulation; performs material handling; at technology readiness level 5.
- census_RXM33-1, adopted to address integration, regulation; performs assembly, steelwork, welding; works on the structural core; at technology readiness level 9.
- census_RXM33-2, adopted to address regulation; performs assembly, material handling, steelwork, welding; works on the structural core; at technology readiness level 7.
- census_RXM4-3, adopted to address regulation; performs 3d printing, assembly, concrete work; works on the structural core; at technology readiness level 7.
